title: [Chapitre] VIII. Analysis situs (quatrième mouture) : notes manuscrites (26/06-04/07/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from pp. 1–65 of this 'quatrième mouture'). M is a set of 'cells' (strata of a tame or cellular space), ordered by ≤, where Y ≤ X means Y lies in the closure of X. X̃ = {Y : Y ≤ X} is the closure of a cell. Two symmetric relations are used. The first, |°|, is antireflexive and means 'open cells X°, Y° are disjoint'. The second, ||, means 'closures disjoint'. On the previous page Grothendieck defines the polarity cosupp°(A) = {Y : A |°| Y} and the closure operator supp° = cosupp°∘cosupp°. The '|°|-supported' parts are the Galois-closed sets S = supp°(S).

This page compares these 'interior' notions with the earlier notion of support from p. 11, which is built from ≤-closures. The image reads cosupp, not 'support':
- cosupp X = {Y ∈ M | Ỹ ⊂ cosupp°(X̃)}
- cosupp A = {Y ∈ M | Ỹ ⊂ cosupp°(Ã)}, where Ã = ∪_{X∈A} X̃ is the smallest ≤-closed part containing A.

Geometrically, Y ∈ cosupp A means every cell of the closure of Y is interior-disjoint from every cell of the closure of A, i.e. closures are disjoint. This is the relation || used on the next page.

Grothendieck then writes 'Donc cosupp A = cosupp°(A) si A = Ã (A fermée pour ≤)'. He strikes it out and labels it 'idiot'. Rightly so: cosupp°(Ã) is in general not ≤-closed. A boundary cell of Y may lie in Ã, so the condition Ỹ ⊂ cosupp°(Ã) is strictly stronger than Y ∈ cosupp°(Ã).

A following paragraph is also struck out. It claimed that supports are the interior supports of ≤-closed parts, and that the earlier 'troubling perplexity' about supports came from working only with supports of closed parts. It added that supp/cosupp are expressible via supp°/cosupp° but not conversely. The deletion presumably follows from the same error.

He then begins 'instructive (somewhat trivial) examples'. If |°| is X ≠ Y (a CW-type situation where distinct open cells are disjoint), then cosupp°(A) = M∖A and supp°(A) = A. So every subset is a support, visualised as the union of the open cells X°, X ∈ A, and the support lattice is the Boolean algebra P(M). The next page treats the opposite extreme, X || Y ⇔ X̄ ∩ Ȳ = ∅. There supports are special closed parts, and Σ_M is studied as a complete lattice with the anti-involution S ↦ ∁S and Sup S_i = supp°(∪S_i).

Purpose: to build a purely combinatorial 'analysis situs' of stratified spaces. Supports (unions of strata that behave like closed or open sets) are described order-theoretically through an orthogonality relation on cells.
errors: The claim 'cosupp A = cosupp°(A) if A is ≤-closed' is false. Grothendieck himself strikes it out and labels it 'idiot': cosupp°(Ã) need not be ≤-closed, so it differs from {Y | Ỹ ⊂ cosupp°(Ã)}.
The struck paragraph identifying the supports with the supp° of closed parts depends on the false identity, and is likewise cancelled.
Otherwise the page is correct. In the example X ≠ Y, supp°(A) = A for all A, so every subset is a support.

ideas.what: Polarity cosupp° defined by a symmetric antireflexive relation on cells; supports are its Galois-closed sets; the complement S ↦ cosupp°(S) gives an orthocomplemented complete lattice Σ_M.
ideas.modern_name: Orthogonality space and its ortholattice of biorthogonally closed sets (polarity / Galois connection; formal concept lattice)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Birkhoff (polarities, 1940); Dacey (1968) and Foulis–Randall (orthogonality spaces, quantum logic); Wille (formal concept analysis, 1982)

ideas.what: Comparing supports defined via open-cell disjointness with supports defined via closure disjointness, using ≤-closures X̃ and Ã.
ideas.modern_name: Closed/open unions of strata in a stratified or cellular poset (Alexandrov topology on the face poset)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Alexandrov (1937); standard in combinatorial topology of CW and regular cell complexes
ideas.where_published: The general theme of tame topology is in Esquisse d'un programme (1984); this specific formalism is not published as far as I know

ideas.what: Trivial example: the relation X ≠ Y gives every subset as a support, i.e. arbitrary unions of open cells.
ideas.modern_name: Boolean algebra of constructible unions of cells

missed.claim: Grothendieck's lattice Σ_M of supports, built from a symmetric antireflexive 'disjointness' relation on strata, is exactly the ortholattice of an orthogonality space as in quantum logic (Dacey, Foulis–Randall). This link between tame stratified topology and orthogonality spaces/ortholattices appears not to be made in the literature. It is a weak point, since the construction itself is standard order theory.
missed.quote: cosupp X = {Y∈M | Ỹ ⊂ cosupp°(X̃)} ... Les supp et cosupp s'expriment ... en termes de supp° et cosupp°, mais l'inverse n'est pas vrai.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is only a potential bridge. It could let one use ortholattice and concept-lattice tools to classify the 'supports' of stratified or o-minimal cell decompositions. It is of marginal significance.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a working page comparing two notions of support in a combinatorial cell-poset setting. It contains an error that Grothendieck himself retracts ('idiot') and a trivial example. The underlying construction is a standard polarity/closure operator.
transcription_corrections: In the displayed formulas the operator is 'cosupp' (written 'cosupp X', 'cosupp A', 'cosupp°'), not 'support'/'supp°'. They should read: cosupp X = {Y∈M | Ỹ ⊂ cosupp°(X̃)} and cosupp A = {Y∈M | Ỹ ⊂ cosupp°(Ã)}. The '{Y∈M | Ỹ ⊂' is a superscript insertion shared by both lines.
The struck line reads: 'Donc cosupp A = cosupp°(A) si A = Ã i.e. A fermée dans M pour ≤', with marginal 'idiot'.

The struck paragraph reads approximately: 'Ainsi, les supports sont les supports intérieurs des parties de M fermées pour ≤ ... La troublante perplexité des supports était causée par le fait qu'il ne travaillait qu'avec les supports de parties fermées. Les supp et cosupp s'expriment ... en termes de supp° et cosupp°, mais l'inverse n'est pas vrai.'
In the example the relation is most likely '|°|' (interior disjointness), not '|!|': 'La relation |°| est la relation X ≠ Y'.
The page number at top is 66 (archive page 75).
